titleStmt.title: Work in Progress: Security-Aware Preemptive Scheduling with Partial Trust for Safety-Critical Embedded Systems

analytic.title: Work in Progress: Security-Aware Preemptive Scheduling with Partial Trust for Safety-Critical Embedded Systems

div.p: Safety-critical embedded systems often have very limited computational capabilities that must be carefully managed to provide the required functionalities. Since such systems are increasingly becoming a target of attacks, there is a need for real-time resource-allocation techniques that are resistant to such attacks. We extend the widely used sporadic task model to additionally enable the representation of certain kinds of security requirements, develop a corresponding scheduling algorithm and associated schedulability test, and experimentally evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm and test.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The complexity of software in contemporary embedded systems, coupled with often ad hoc methods that are used in their development, poses a substantial risk of software vulnerabilities. In safety-critical real-time systems, the exploitation of these vulnerabilities by malicious actors can result in severe outcomes. Consequently, there is a general agreement on the importance of integrating security considerations into the design process of safety-critical embedded systems. Prior work [1]- [3] has explored approaches for achieving security in safety-critical real-time embedded systems by:

• explicitly modeling threats by extending formal frameworks for real-time workload specification; and • adapting established techniques for proving timing correctness to these enhanced models, and so ensuring that both timing and security properties are verified as correct.
This paper outlines our recent research in this area.

Workload model. We consider the scheduling of real-time systems that can be modeled as a collection of independent recurrent processes, each represented using the widely-used 3parameter sporadic task model [4], that are to be implemented upon a single shared preemptive processor.

Threat model. Our threat model draws inspiration from the one proposed by Nasri et al. [5] -it considers that some of the tasks present in the system may be malicious 'attacker' tasks that seek to obtain some information about other potential 'victim' tasks, via the side channel of examining the state of shared resources (specifically, cache) after the victim task has completed execution. Thus, each context switch is a potential security risk; given the prevalence of preemptive scheduling in embedded real-time systems, preemptions must be carefully managed to mitigate vulnerabilities.

Security assumptions. The implementation platform must be capable of maintaining certain properties if it is to offer meaningful security guarantees. We assume that the scheduler implementation can reliably perform the following three runtime operations in a secure manner: (i) selecting the next task to execute; (ii) allocating an execution budget to the selected task; and (iii) enforcing these budgets, preventing any task from running beyond its allocated time. Additionally, task specifications are stored in trusted memory, ensuring that attackers cannot deceive the scheduler about task parameters.

Prior work. One approach to preventing such attacks is for each potential victim task to perform explicit clean-up operations (e.g., overwriting used buffer locations) before yielding the processor, adding overhead. Prior work [1]- [3] extends the sporadic task model to represent this security mechanism with varying generality. Scheduling algorithms and schedulability tests are provided for each model, ensuring (i) correct run-time behavior with all timing constraints met, and (ii) security against the modeled threat.

This work. In this work, we revisit this "cleanup-uponcontext-switching" approach of [1]- [3]. We propose a new workload model, the SEC (for Sporadic with Exclusion Constraints) task model, which enables a more nuanced expression of threats than previous models in [1]- [3]. Unlike prior approaches where every task considers all others as potential attackers, our model allows each task to specify which other tasks it does not trust, treating them as potential attackers. We propose a simple algorithm to address these vulnerabilities: instead of allowing preemption with overhead for clean-up, we prevent preemption by any task flagged as a potential attacker. We present an optimal schedulability test for this approach and evaluate its effectiveness through simulations on synthetic workloads.

Organization. The paper is organized as follows: Section II presents the system model and design rationale. Section III covers securing the model against cache-based attacks Simulation results are in Section IV, and Section VI summarizes our contributions and their relation to prior work.

div.head: II. THE SEC TASK MODEL
div.p: In this section we specify the problem that we are considering in this paper, by proposing a formal model and explaining how it differs from the model considered in prior work [1]- [3].

We propose a new task model, the Sporadic with Exclusion Constraints (SEC) task model, as a generalization of the sporadic task model [4] that is widely used in real-time computing. In the sporadic task model, a real-time system consists of a set of independent recurrent processes running on a shared platform; in this paper, we assume the shared platform is a single fully preemptive processor. Each recurrent process is modeled as a sporadic task τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) that is characterized by a worst-case execution requirement (WCET) C i ∈ N, a relative deadline D i ∈ N, and a period T i ∈ N. A sporadic task generates an unbounded sequence of jobs, with each arriving at least T i time units apart. Each job executes for at most C i time units and must complete execution by its deadline, which is D i time units after arrival. A sporadic task system consists of multiple such tasks.

Our SEC task model builds on the sporadic task model by further characterizing each task τ i with an untrusted list L i of all the other tasks in the system that τ i considers to be potential attacker tasks (with itself the victim of the attack):
div.formula: L i def = {τ j | τ j is a potential attacker task of τ i }.(1)
div.p: Hence a SEC task system Γ is specified as follows:
div.formula: Γ def = n i=1 τ i = (C i , D i , T i , L i )(2)
div.p: where each C i , D i , and T i ∈ N, and each L i ⊊ Γ. (We assume that the WCET parameter C i of each task τ i includes the execution duration needed for the cleanup operation that must be performed upon job completion.)

The SEC task model provides a more detailed representation of the attacker-victim relationship, generalizing earlier models in [1]- [3]. This is evident since the expressiveness of the earlier models is achieved by setting each

But the SEC task model allows us to model additional attackervictim relationship possibilities, such as (i) a group of tasks that all trust one another other (all such tasks are excluded from each others' untrusted lists), or (ii) distinct security "levels" that are totally ordered (each task's untrusted list will include all tasks with lower security levels).

div.head: III. DEFENDING AGAINST ATTACK
div.p: In this section we describe our algorithm for ensuring that each task τ i is secured from attacks by any task on its untrusted list L i . We start out in Section III-A with some background from real-time schedulability theory that is needed Let τ1, τ2, . . . , τn denote the sporadic tasks, and R1, R2, . . . , Rm the non-preemptable resources, in a resource-sharing real-time system. 1) Prior to run-time, each resource Rj is assigned a ceiling Π(Rj), which is set equal to the minimum relative deadline parameter of any task that may access it:
div.formula: Π(Rj) = min{Di | τi uses Rj (for > 0 time units)} 2)
div.p: A system ceiling is computed each instant during run-time. This is set equal to the minimum ceiling of any resource that is currently being held by some job. 3) At any instant in time, a job generated by τi may begin execution only if it is the earliest-deadline active job, and Di is strictly less than the system ceiling. for describing our algorithm. In Section III-B we provide a high-level overview of our approach; the details are provided in Section III-C, alongside a schedulability-analysis algorithm for determining whether a given SEC task system is guaranteed to always meet all deadlines when scheduled by our algorithm.

div.head: A. BACKGROUND: SHARED RESOURCES
div.p: This paper focuses on preemptive uniprocessor scheduling, but notes that real-time systems often run on uniprocessor platforms with multiple serially reusable, non-preemptable resources alongside the preemptive processor. Each job requires the processor in order to execute; some jobs may simultaneously additionally need exclusive access to one or more of the resources during part or all of their execution. Adopting the terminology of [6], we will refer to real-time systems that may be modeled as collections of such resource-sharing sporadic tasks as resource-sharing real-time systems. The Stack Resource Policy (SRP) [7] is widely used for arbitrating access to such shared resources; it has been shown [7] to be an optimal (scheduling + resource-allocation) policy when used alongside EDF. This paper assumes reasonable familiarity with the Stack Resource Policy (SRP). When combined with EDF (referred to as EDF+SRP), the SRP rules for determining execution rights are summarized in Figure 1.

div.head: B. OVERVIEW OF APPROACH
div.p: The approach we propose in this paper to prevent a potential attacker task that appears in a task's untrusted list from subjecting that task to an attack is to prohibit preemption of an executing task by any task that appears in its untrusted list: if a job of τ i is executing at some point in time during runtime, then no job of any τ j ∈ L i may preempt it. To achieve this, we transform a given SEC task system into a resource-sharing sporadic task system by adding shared resources to model the non-preemptivity constraints: if τ j appears in τ i 's untrusted list L i in the SEC task system, we introduce a shared resource R ij that is shared between tasks τ i and τ j (and is not accessed by any other task), on which the duration of τ i 's critical section is equal to its WCET C i and the duration of τ j 's critical section Algorithm 1: Converting an SEC task system to a resource-sharing sporadic task system 1 for each τ i ∈ Γ do 2 for each τ j ∈ L i do 3 define a resource R ij that is shared between τ i and τ j 4 let τ i 's critical section on R ij have execution duration C i 5 let τ j 's critical section on R ij have execution duration 0 is zero. During runtime each job of τ i claims all such shared resources R ij for all τ j ∈ L i prior to beginning execution, and only yields these resources upon completion. EDF+SRP guarantees that no task τ j in L i can execute between the start and completion of τ i 's job, thereby ensuring that τ i 's job is secured from attacks by any task in L i .

div.head: C. ALGORITHM AND ANALYSIS
div.p: We explain how to determine if a task system Γ, defined by the SEC task model, can always meet deadlines under our approach. As detailed in Section III-B, we transform Γ into a resource-sharing system Γ ′ and schedule it using EDF+SRP. We show that Γ ′ is schedulable under EDF+SRP to meet all deadlines if and only if Γ is schedulable and satisfies the security requirement that no task job is preempted by jobs from tasks in its untrusted list. Since there are standard tests (such as the ones in [6], [7]) for determining whether a resourcesharing sporadic task system is schedulable by EDF+SRP to always meet all deadlines, it remains to specify how to construct Γ ′ from the given Γ. Since Γ ′ is a resource-sharing real-time system and "a resource-sharing real-time system is specified by specifying the [. . . ] non-preemptable serially reusable resources [. . . ] and the [. . . ] sporadic tasks [. . . ] that comprise it" [6], we must describe how the resources and sporadic tasks comprising Γ ′ are obtained from Γ. Before doing so, we point out an easily-verified property of EDF scheduling on preemptive processors that can be used to trim the untrusted lists without compromising security: Lemma 1. If the relative deadline D j of sporadic task τ j is ≥ the relative deadline D i of sporadic task τ i , then no job of τ j will ever preempt the execution of any job of τ i .

Proof. Under EDF, a job only preempts another job upon arrival, and it only does so if its (absolute) deadline is earlier than the deadline of the currently-executing job. But if τ i is the currently executing job and D j ≥ D i , then the deadline of a newly-arrived job of τ j cannot be earlier than the deadline of a currently-executing (and hence already-arrived) job of τ i .

Lemma 1 enables trimming each task's untrusted list L i by removing tasks τ j with D j ≥ D i . Then, Algorithm 1 generates the resource-sharing system Γ ′ from Γ, followed by schedulability tests (e.g., in [6], [7]) to validate Γ ′ .

Extensions. We use EDF+SRP for runtime scheduling, but similar analysis applies to fixed-priority scheduling. Γ ′ could be scheduled with FP+SRP or FP+PCP [8], using the corresponding schedulability analysis. The only difference in obtaining Γ ′ from Γ is the trimming pre-processing, where tasks τ j with lower priority than τ i are removed from L i , as they cannot preempt τ i 's jobs under FP scheduling.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: The section discusses the evaluation of the proposed Sporadic with Exclusion Constraints (SEC) task model and its associated scheduling algorithm. The goal is to assess the model's effectiveness and practicality by comparing it with traditional scheduling approaches, such as fully preemptive EDF scheduling. Key performance metrics, like schedulability across different system utilizations, are analyzed to demonstrate how the SEC model improves system reliability and security. The goal is to demonstrate SEC as a viable solution for real-time applications with strict timing and security guarantees.

div.head: A. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
div.p: All our algorithms, including the generation of the SEC task system, Γ, its conversion to a resource sharing realtime system, Γ ′ , the EDF+SRP scheduling algorithm and the schedulability tests, were implemented in python. The evaluations were conducted over 1000 randomly generated task systems, each containing 5 tasks. These task sets were generated using the UUniFast algorithm [9], which is widely used for creating task sets with a specified total utilization. Each task is defined by its worst-case execution time C i , relative deadline D i , period T i , and an untrusted list L i . The exclusion probability p, which dictates the likelihood of a task being considered a potential attacker by another task, is provided as an input parameter, enabling exploration of different untrusted list configurations. We assume that the Worst-Case Execution Time (C i ) for each task includes post-execution clean-up, ensuring that our timing analysis covers both computational tasks and security measures against vulnerabilities like cache-based attacks.

The Untrusted List Construction. For each task set Γ, untrusted lists are constructed based on the input probability p. If p = 0, no tasks are untrusted, allowing free preemption imitating a fully trusted environment, equivalent to preemptive scheduling. If p = 1, every task views all others as untrusted leading to a highly restrictive environment, like non-preemptive scheduling. For intermediate values of p, (0 < p < 1), tasks randomly include other tasks in their untrusted lists, ensuring each task's list is a subset of others, but never includes itself.
The resulting configuration represents a more realistic partial trust environment where some tasks are restricted from preempting others based on the assigned probability.

Resource Initialization. We also implemented an algorithm to handle resource initialization and the definition of critical sections based on the untrusted lists. This process is crucial for mimicking the non-preemptivity constraints as shared resources, ensuring that tasks listed in each other's untrusted lists cannot preempt one another. The algorithm iterates through each task in the task set, defining a shared resource for each untrusted task pair. For each task τ i , it checks its untrusted list L i and defines a resource R ij for each pair (τ i , τ j ). The critical section for τ i on R ij is its execution duration C i , while τ j 's critical section is zero. This approach models exclusion constraints, preventing task τ j from preempting task τ i during execution.

Resources are initialized by iterating over each task and its untrusted list, creating a unique resource R ij for each pair (τ i , τ j ) with properties like system ceiling, the task holding the resource, and critical sections. This ensures exclusion constraints and prevents preemption-based attacks. Thus, the task system Γ is transformed into Γ ′ with initialized resources and critical sections. Its schedulability is then tested to ensure deadline compliance under the constraints, verifying the SEC model's reliability and security.

div.head: B. SCHEDULABILITY RESULTS
div.p: We focused on assessing the schedulability ratios of the EDF+SRP algorithm. Schedulability tests were conducted by varying the system utilization levels and the probabilities of tasks appearing in the untrusted lists. This approach allowed us to observe the impact of exclusion constraints on the schedulability of the system under different configurations. For p = 0 (traditional preemptive EDF), the schedulability ratio remains at 1 across all utilizations. As p increases, the ratio drops: for p = 0.25, it starts high at lower utilizations but falls to 0.513 at full utilization; for p = 0.5, it declines further to 0.415; at p = 0.75, it reaches 0.397, and at p = 1, the ratio drops to 0.396. These results show that while the SEC model maintains high schedulability at lower utilizations, performance decreases with higher exclusion probability and system load.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: By integrating timing and security properties into a single model, we extend real-time scheduling theory to guarantee security in resource-constrained embedded systems. Our proposed algorithm ensures both timing and security correctness, building on prior work in real-time scheduling for resourcesharing systems. The results validate the SEC model's design, balancing security and timing guarantees. The model performs optimally under preemptive conditions, maintaining high schedulability at low to moderate utilizations. However, as exclusion probability p and system load increase, schedulability declines, highlighting the trade-off between security and performance. These findings emphasize the importance of carefully tuning exclusion probabilities to optimize system performance while maintaining security. This work defends against potential attacker tasks by preventing preemption from such tasks. Future research will explore more sophisticated defenses, such as allowing preemptions with associated runtime overhead, as studied in [1]- [3]. In this context, our current model becomes a special case where preemption overhead is infinite. Additionally, we plan to extend the model to support more complex real-time task models, including sporadic tasks with job chains or directed acyclic graphs, each with distinct untrusted task lists.
